definition: The ASTM International committee, formed in 1978, that writes the main North American amusement ride standards.
An ASTM document that sets out an agreed way of doing something, such as designing or inspecting a ride.
A pre-existing ride design exempted from a new design standard because its safe operating history is documented.
A change to a ride significant enough that the design standard applies to it as if it were new.
The European standard for fairground and amusement park rides, split since 2019 into design, operation and inspection parts.
The international ride safety standard from ISO/TC 254, closely aligned with EN 13814.
The UK ADIPS certificate issued after pre-use or annual inspection confirming a ride may be operated.
An organisation registered under a scheme such as ADIPS to review designs and inspect rides independently.
A permanent ride at a park, which in the United States falls outside federal CPSC jurisdiction.
The structured process of finding hazards, estimating how bad and how likely they are, and reducing them until acceptable.
Failure Mode and Effects Analysis, a component-by-component list of how things can fail and what would happen.
A programmable controller with redundant, self-checking hardware rated for safety-critical functions.
A control-system condition, such as all restraints locked, that must be true before dispatch is allowed.
Control logic that divides a track into sections and never lets two trains occupy the same one.
A design whose default state on loss of power or signal is a safe one, such as a spring-applied brake.
A second independent means of performing a critical safety function in case the first fails.
An IEC 61508 rating from 1 to 4 that caps how often a safety function may fail dangerously.
The ISO 13849 rating from a to e that expresses the reliability required of a safety-related control function.
The volume a rider's outstretched limbs could occupy, swept along the ride path, which must stay clear of structure.
A latching red control that brings a ride to a defined safe stop and must be deliberately reset.
A category assigned from a seat's accelerations that dictates the type and redundancy of restraint required.
Methods such as ultrasonic or magnetic particle inspection that find cracks and thinning without damaging the part.
A notice from a manufacturer or regulator telling all owners of a ride type about a fault or required check.
A workplace where honest errors can be reported without punishment while reckless acts are still addressed.
James Reason's picture of layered defences with holes; harm only passes when the holes line up.
